# Roadmap stages

Read when proposing stages at the Review Gate and when adding them on acceptance; the mode file says which stages to propose. An example: `examples-data.md`.

Stages live in `docs/roadmap.md`. A stage is an outcome the user agreed: what they can do when it's done, such as "Data + stats" or "See my spending". It is coarse and unsized. **Don't size it:** no task estimates, no pipeline counts, no splitting a stage because it looks big. Two stages differ by outcome, never by size. Once a stage's pipelines are approved, `build-planning` cuts it into build-sized milestones (`M<n>`), each a vertical slice it can run end to end, and owns those rows.

**Add stages only when the user accepts** (Phase 4). Each stage takes its ID from `dt next-id S` (`dt` as defined in `../SKILL.md`), a short name, and its Source. Leave the Status* cell empty, then run `dt roadmap`, which fills it. Under the tables, add a `## S<n>: <Name>` section with one plain-English `**Outline:**` line (what the user can do when the stage is done) and one `**Skills:**` line.

**Stage skills and references.** The `**Skills:**` line is the one record of which skills serve a stage; later skills start from it and `build-planning` checks each one lands on a milestone and then a task. Propose the skills whose descriptions fit the stage (project `.claude/skills/*/SKILL.md` and the installed skills in your context), and ask once: "Route profile-report and significance-check to S2? [yes / edit]". None fit → `**Skills:** —`. Also offer each `references_unassigned` entry that serves the stage ("RF-02 and RF-03 (boosting) → S3? [yes / edit]"). On acceptance, write the line and set `**Milestones:**` on each RF entry the user assigned to the stage ID (`—` becomes `S3`; otherwise append). Those two fields are all you write in the roadmap sections and `docs/references.md`.

If `docs/roadmap.md` doesn't exist, create it:

```markdown
# [Project Name] — Roadmap

**Last updated:** YYYY-MM-DD

| Stage | Name | Source | Status* |
|---|---|---|---|
| S1 | [Name] | brief | |

*Written by `dt roadmap` from doc statuses and todo checkboxes; never hand-edited.

## S1: [Name]
**Outline:** [What the user can do when this stage is done, in one sentence.]
**Skills:** [skill names routed to this stage, comma-separated, or —]
```

Add stages; never renumber, reorder or edit existing ones. A roadmap from before stages has only a milestone table (with a Source column): add the stage table above it for the first new stage, and leave the old rows as they are.

# RL Lab

**Status:** Draft · **Last updated:** 2026-10-18

## The problem
Reinforcement learning (RL) is how an agent learns by trial and error from rewards. It is easy to read about and hard to really understand. Library code hides the parts that matter, and tutorials stop once the agent "works". The fastest way to learn it is to build small agents from scratch, in small 2D game environments, where each one teaches one idea and you can see it learn.

## Who it's for
Me: a solid Python programmer with some NumPy and PyTorch, who knows the basics of Q-learning (learning the value of each action in each state) and wants to learn RL by building it.

## Goals
1. For each environment, I can explain in my own words why the agent learns, and why each part of the algorithm matters.
2. Every agent is shown to learn: its learning curve beats a random agent and a simple scripted agent on the same games.
3. I can watch a replay of any trained agent playing.
4. A new environment reuses a shared core (environment interface, training loop, logging, replay viewer, learning curves) instead of starting over.

## Constraints
- Laptop CPU only, and under about an hour of training per environment.
- Free tools only.
- Evenings and weekends, a few weeks per environment, no deadline.
- Learning algorithms are written from scratch, not taken from a library.

## What success looks like
- The first environment, Snake, has an agent whose learning curve clearly beats both baselines, plus a replay of it playing.
- Turning off a key part of the agent visibly hurts its learning, and I can say why.
- The second environment, whatever it is, plugs into the shared core with small changes.

## What we're betting on
- Small, hand-picked descriptions of the game state ("danger ahead", "food to the left") are enough for an agent to learn well within an hour on a CPU.
- A shared core designed while Snake is the only example will still fit the next environment without a rewrite.
- Writing the algorithms myself teaches more than tuning a library would.

## Not doing
- Learning from raw pixels or the full grid image: much slower, and not the lesson I'm after.
- Comparing against library implementations, for now: a later step, once my own version works.
- Fancy views such as heatmaps of the agent's values: learning curves and replays are enough.
- Planning environments beyond Snake: the next one is chosen once Snake is done.
- Mastering Snake: agents that see only nearby danger tend to trap themselves, and that limit is fine.
- GPUs or paid compute: everything has to run on a laptop.

I've written a Draft brief for the whole RL Lab at `docs/brief.md` (448 words).

- **Problem:** RL is easy to read about and hard to really understand. Building small agents from scratch in 2D environments, one idea per environment, is the fastest way to learn it.
- **Top goal:** for each environment, you can explain why the agent learns and why each part of the algorithm matters (Goal 1). Goal 2 makes it checkable: the learning curve has to beat a random agent and a scripted agent on the same games.
- **Biggest Not Doing item:** no learning from raw pixels or the full grid image.

The brief covers the whole lab, so it says nothing Snake-specific beyond what success looks like. The details of the direction you picked (2 + 4 + 6: hand-picked state features, switches to turn off parts of the agent, scored against baselines) and your 1-hour limit go into the spec next. Library choices and "from scratch on a laptop CPU" go into the architecture.

**How your words map into the brief:**
- "an RL lab of little 2D environments…" UR-01 and "learn RL by building" UR-02 → The problem
- "Solid Python, decent NumPy/PyTorch…" UR-07 → Who it's for
- "I can explain why it works" UR-12 → Goal 1
- "no budget beyond free tools" UR-15 → Constraints, "Free tools only"
- "Evenings/weekends, a few weeks…" UR-16 → Constraints
- "compare against libraries later" UR-09 → Not doing, "for now: a later step"
- "Nothing beyond Snake for now" UR-19 and "just the first piece" UR-03 → Not doing, "Planning environments beyond Snake"
- No brief-owned requests are left open. The 12 spec and architecture requests wait for those steps.

**Proposed roadmap stage, added once you accept:**

> **S1: Snake + shared core.** You can train a DQN you wrote yourself on Snake in under an hour, see its learning curve beat the random and scripted agents, switch off parts of the agent to see what breaks, and watch a replay. All of it runs on a shared core the next environment can reuse.
> **Skills:** `null-hypothesis-testing` (to show "beats the baselines" across several training seeds isn't just luck), `dataviz` (learning curves).

Route those two skills to S1? [yes / edit]

**Accept the brief** (a yes also adds S1 and commits), or tell me what to change.
